sentences.text: Paludititan was a titanosaurian sauropod belonging to the class Saurischia and the parent group Eutitanosauria.
This animal stood only about 2 meters tall at the shoulder, with Gregory S. Paul estimating its total length at 6 meters and weight at one ton in 2016.

Its back vertebrae featured unique ridges that ran parallel rather than touching, and the ischium peduncle had a triangular process forming a buttress over the ilium, though this trait is no longer seen as unique to the species.
When first described, this skeleton was the most complete sauropod ever found in Romania.
It shared its home on Hațeg Island with other dwarf dinosaurs like Magyarosaurus, Telmatosaurus, and Zalmoxes.
The genus Paludititan and the species Paludititan nalatzensis were named and described in 2010 by Zoltán Csiki and colleagues.
The specific name nalatzensis honors the discovery location Nălațvad, where researchers initially suspected the bones belonged to Magyarosaurus dacus before justifying a separate name.
The holotype, a partial skeleton lacking the skull, was found in the Sânpetru Formation and included dorsal and tail vertebrae, chevrons, pelvis parts, a femur fragment, and toe claws.
Although the remains were not articulated, their close association suggests they belong to a single individual, and there are currently two recorded fossil occurrences of the taxon.
The island ecosystem included endemic dinosaurs such as the nodosaurid Struthiosaurus and the avialan Balaur, while the top predator was the giant pterosaur Hatzegopteryx.
Paludititan was classified within the Titanosauria in 2010 as a relatively advanced titanosaurian, though its closest relatives remain unclear.
It was considered a probable member of the Lithostrotia clade, a sister species to the South American Epachthosaurus, and later placed in the Saltasauridae family.
This creature lived on the island ecosystem known as Hațeg Island during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Researchers initially considered the possibility that the skeleton belonged to Magyarosaurus dacus, a contemporary sauropod from the same habitat.
